Top 3 Temasek-Backed Blue Chips Beating the Market YTD
article:
October was a down month for Singapore stocks, but the broader picture looks brighter when viewed over the year.
The
SPDR Straits Times Index ETF
(SGX: ES3), which mirrors Singapore’s
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI), delivered a total return of 19.2% for the year to end-October, despite the month’s decline.
Three Temasek-linked blue chips did even better.
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05) returned 35%.
Singapore Technologies Engineering Ltd
(SGX: S63), or ST Engineering, delivered a return of 23%, while
Singapore Exchange Limited
(SGX: S68), or SGX, returned 22%.
All three figures include dividends and cover the first 10 months of 2026.
Temasek, a global investment company headquartered in Singapore, owned 28% of DBS and 51% of ST Engineering as at 31 March 2026.
Its link to SGX is less direct: Temasek owns SEL Holdings, which held a 23.35% stake in SGX as at 1 September 2026.
Beyond their Temasek connections, the three companies have two things in common.
In their latest results, ST Engineering and SGX grew profit faster than revenue (SGX only after excluding one-off items), and DBS did so until its 3Q2026 results.
They also gave investors a clearer view of future payouts.
Investors may be rewarding that combination.
What does SGX offer dividend investors?
SGX
offers a growing ordinary dividend, with a timetable for future increases.
For the year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2026), SGX grew net revenue by 13.9% year on year (YoY) to S$1.5 billion, as securities daily average traded value rose 34.9% to S$1.8 billion and Equities – Cash revenue increased 28.1% to S$502.9 million.
Reported net profit grew by a more modest 7.8% to S$698.4 million, held back by a S$53.4 million goodwill impairment on Scientific Beta and weaker investment gains.
Excluding these items, adjusted net profit rose 24.6% to S$759.5 million.
SGX ended the year with S$1.8 billion in cash against S$628.2 million in borrowings, while operating cash flow reached S$870.7 million and capital expenditure stood at S$94.2 million.
For FY2026, SGX declared ordinary dividends of S$0.445 per share and a one-off dividend of S$0.125 per share, bringing the total to S$0.570, up from S$0.375 a year earlier.
Management has guided for quarterly dividend increases of S$0.0025 per share through FY2028 and plans to repay all its debt in FY2027.
However, trading activity can fade as quickly as it picks up, while FY2027 expenses are expected to rise by 6% to 8%.
Can DBS keep growing as its trading income slumps?
The customer business is still growing.
The trading desk is another matter.
By the end of October, investors had DBS’s second-quarter results (2Q2026), which showed net profit growing 9% on a 6% rise in total income.
The 3Q2026 results, released on 5 November 2026, look different.
Total income for
Singapore’s largest bank
by market capitalisation slipped 1.5% YoY to S$5.85 billion.
Net interest income rose 3.7% to S$3.71 billion, even as the net interest margin narrowed to 1.87% from 1.96%.
Customer loans grew 9.5% to S$478.6 billion.
Here’s the thing: markets trading non-interest income fell to S$17 million from S$419 million.
Net fee and commission income still rose 6% to S$1.43 billion.
Net profit fell 4.8% to S$2.81 billion.
For the first nine months, net profit reached a record S$8.82 billion.
The non-performing loan (NPL) ratio fell to 0.9% from 1.0%.
The board declared an ordinary dividend of S$0.66 per share, up from S$0.60 a year ago.
The capital return dividend stayed at S$0.15 per share.
Management expects mid-single-digit total income growth in 2027, warning of a more uncertain outlook amid elevated energy prices, tighter financial conditions and geopolitical risks.
Is ST Engineering’s dividend on firm ground?
Free cash flow offers some reassurance, but the balance sheet deserves a closer look.
For 1H2026,
ST Engineering
grew revenue by 11.1% YoY to S$6.6 billion and net profit by 27.1% to S$512.1 million.
Commercial Aerospace revenue increased 15%, supported by higher engine maintenance, engine housing and spares sales, while net finance costs fell 14.9%.
Free cash flow improved to S$591.6 million from S$484.6 million a year earlier.
The group paid S$0.04 per share for 1Q2026 and declared S$0.05 for 2Q2026, bringing its half-year dividend to S$0.09, up from S$0.08, with another S$0.05 planned for 3Q2026.
However, cash fell to S$255.3 million as at 30 June 2026, from S$576.4 million at the end of 2025, while total borrowings, including lease liabilities, stood at S$4.7 billion.
The order book reached a record S$35.7 billion, with about S$5.7 billion due for delivery over the rest of 2026.
Get Smart: Check the return against the profit growth
Compare each stock’s total return with its latest profit growth to see how the two stack up.
ST Engineering returned 23%, against net profit growth of 27.1%, while SGX returned 22%, against adjusted profit growth of 24.6%.
DBS tells a different story, with its 35% return well ahead of quarterly profit growth of 9% in 2Q2026.
The 3Q2026 results widened that gap, with net profit down 4.8%.
In other words, investors may now be paying more for each dollar of DBS’s profit.
The periods differ, so treat this as a rough guide rather than a like-for-like comparison.
When share returns outpace earnings growth, future gains may depend on profits catching up.
Before buying these stocks, ask yourself: can their businesses keep growing into their current valuations?
Many Singapore stocks fall behind inflation, which means your money quietly loses strength over time. Dividend stocks have a very different track record. Some continued delivering 6% to 13% every year across the toughest market conditions.

title: Asian stocks, bonds to drop as Fed hike bets mount
article:
(Nov 11) : Asian stocks and bonds were poised to fall after hotter-than-expected US inflation drove losses on Wall Street and fueled bets that the Federal Reserve may hike interest rates more aggressively to tame prices.

Equity-index futures for South Korea, Japan, Hong Kong and Australia pointed to losses. Benchmark government bonds in Australia and New Zealand fell in early trading on Wednesday. The S&P 500 halted back-to-back gains, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 fell 0.6%. The dollar rose and gold tumbled.

Consumer prices, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3% in October from a month earlier, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data, topping estimates for a third straight month. Overall CPI jumped 0.4% as the cost of essentials climbed across the board.

The data triggered a selloff in Treasuries, with the rate-sensitive short-dated bonds hit the hardest. Two-year yields jumped 17 basis points to 4.73%, the most in 19 months. Money markets are now pricing in the Fed to raise rates by a quarter point at its meeting next month, with some chance of an even larger move. Futures are baking in about three quarter-point hikes by June.

Following the release of CPI data, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said more rapid rate hikes may be needed this winter to calm inflation. Her remarks followed earlier comments from Governor Christopher Waller that a half-point rate increase in December may be warranted.

“The Fed could push for a more-aggressive tightening cycle with CPI continuing to print strong,” said Lindsay Rosner at Goldman Sachs Asset Management. “A December hike is our firm base case despite wider AI jitters, and stubborn inflation means we cannot rule out further hikes in 2027.”

See also: OpenAI third quarter revenue soars nearly 50% to US$10 billion

The prospect of aggressive Fed hikes threatens to derail a nascent recovery in stocks that were whipsawed in the wake of Democratic sweep of the US Congress in the midterms. For bonds, the selloff marked a reversal of a rally that began early last month as tech stocks slipped on worries about the sustainability of the artificial-intelligence boom.

The hot CPI print is a “headwind” for risk assets with “higher front-end yields and a stronger dollar weighing on equity valuations,” said Jeff Schulze, head investment strategist at Franklin Templeton Institute.

Investors are also weighing news that Anthropic PBC is targeting US$1.4 trillion in fully diluted market value through its initial public offering. CoreWeave Inc. reported quarterly earnings that topped analysts’ estimates and boosted its annual forecast, easing investor concerns about the debt-laden business suffering a slowdown.

See also: Stocks, bonds fall as Fed-hike chorus grows louder

Shares of SoftBank Group Corp. will be in focus after it swung to a 1.12 trillion yen (US$7.1 billion) loss in its fiscal second quarter after writing down non-refundable advance payments for its US data-center projects.

Elsewhere, Brent crude fell for a second straight day to settle near US$92 a barrel on expectations of further de-escalation in the Iran war. Brent is still up almost 50% this year but the oil market has seen a dramatic turnaround in November, with prices tumbling from a six-month high.

title: OpenAI third quarter revenue soars nearly 50% to US$10 billion
article:
(Nov 11) : OpenAI’s quarterly revenue hit US$10 billion for the first time in the three months ending in September, according to a person familiar with the matter, driven by strong demand for its latest artificial intelligence software.

The ChatGPT maker’s revenue increased nearly 50% from the prior quarter and nearly threefold from the same period a year earlier, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the information is not public. The financial details were shared with investors during a call on Tuesday.

After slipping behind longtime rival Anthropic PBC this year by some measures, OpenAI has regained momentum with competitive new AI models, aggressive price cuts and a greater focus on AI agents to help customers automate work. OpenAI’s business has shown signs of accelerating at a moment when Anthropic’s revenue growth has begun to slow somewhat.

Anthropic, which is nearing a landmark Wall Street debut, reported third-quarter revenue of about US$17 billion. The rate of growth from the second quarter slowed to around 47%, compared to a more than 140% increase in the previous quarter. (OpenAI and Anthropic have historically calculated revenue figures differently.)

OpenAI is in the process of completing a new round of funding at a US$1.25 trillion valuation after delaying plans to go public until next year. OpenAI recently completed an initial US$11 billion part of that round, Bloomberg News previously reported.

See also: Stocks, bonds fall as Fed-hike chorus grows louder

Anthropic is targeting a US$1.4 trillion valuation for its public listing later this month.

title: Stocks, bonds fall as Fed-hike chorus grows louder
article:
(Nov 11) : Wall Street doubled down on wagers the Federal Reserve will need to lift rates more aggressively, with stocks and bonds falling as inflation worries spurred fresh warnings from officials.

A strong consumer price index fueled bets on a quarter-point December Fed hike, with traders projecting some chance of a larger move. Treasury two-year yields jumped the most since April 2025. The S&P 500 halted back-to-back gains. The dollar rose. In late hours, CoreWeave Inc. gave a solid outlook, easing fears about the debt-laden business suffering a slowdown.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a half-point December hike may be needed. That was followed by remarks from Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, who backed at least two more quarter-point increases, adding those may be necessary at a quicker pace than officials have moved.

“The Fed could push for a more-aggressive tightening cycle with CPI continuing to print strong,” said Lindsay Rosner at Goldman Sachs Asset Management. “A December hike is our firm base case despite wider AI jitters, and stubborn inflation means we cannot rule out further hikes in 2027.”

Even if the Fed decides to lift rates by a quarter point at its upcoming meeting, the risk of stickier near-term inflation argues for hiking at both the December and January meetings with the risk of another in March, according to Tiffany Wilding at Pacific Investment Management Co.

“A Fed policy rate hike in December appears quite likely and the question is more about whether it will be a quarter point hike or a half point,” said Rick Rieder at BlackRock.

See also: Stocks climb as buyers step in despite Nvidia woes

While financial conditions have been adjusted by markets in rapid fashion, inflation still stayed very high on the minds of openly communicative Fed officials over the past couple of weeks, he added.

“With the near-term trend looking worse, a December Fed hike is a given unless financial conditions tighten materially further or markets are very volatile on the eve of the meeting,” noted Krishna Guha at Evercore. “The larger question is why inflation has come in hotter in recent months, and what this means for policy in 2027.”

A December hike looks locked in, but an outsized move should require evidence that inflation is accelerating decisively, expectations are becoming unanchored or the economy is overheating, said Seema Shah at Principal Asset Management.

See also: Asian stocks brace for selloff as AI rout deepens

“We are not there yet,” Shah noted.
